item.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
item.description:
In the frantic hours after Israelis cast their ballots on Tuesday, early exit polls briefly suggested that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reign might finally be coming to an end. But as official tallies filtered into Wednesday morning, political reality emerged: while Netanyahu fell short of an outright parliamentary majority, he remains firmly in control of Israel’s political destiny. With roughly 71-77% of the ballots counted in the election for the 26th Knesset, the Central Elections Committee reported that Netanyahu’s Right-wing and religious alliance stood at around 54 seats, which is short of the 61 required for a majority in the 120-seat legislature. The primary opposition, the anti-Netanyahu “change bloc” led by former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, lagged further behind at roughly 47 seats, even with turnout surging to 77.7%, Israel’s highest since 1999. item.title: Spain demands answers after deadliest train disaster in over a decade
item.description:
Two high-speed trains crashed in Spain Wednesday morning, leaving at least 68 people dead and another 80 people injured. The trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. on the high-speed line that links Madrid with Spain’s Andalusia region. Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente faulted a failed control system for Wednesday morning’s crash. The control system in the Spanish town Urda failed, which caused six trains to stop. One train, however, was reportedly allowed to restart and then hit a stopped train at a high speed. Puente said the decision to allow the train to restart was “inexplicable.” The deadly collision marks the second train crash in Spain this year. In January, 45 people were killed in another high-speed train collision. The affected trains are understood to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, making it 544 people in total on board of both train ( 11:00 ). item.title: In North Carolina, a ‘Mountain Democrat’ Vies for Residents Still Hurting From Helene
item.description:
Lunch hour was busy at the Haywood County Public Library in Canton, North Carolina, where the midterm election wasn’t the only thing on people’s minds as they cast early ballots on October 19. The region has seen a lot of natural disasters in the past few years, and many residents are still rebuilding after Hurricane Helene. Repeated flooding has unsettled Sandra Moody, a straight-ticket Republican voter. “Well, we’re not weather people,” Moody said with a hoarse laugh, “but these floods that keep coming — they’re supposed to be 500-year floods. You’re like, ‘What is going on?’” Two years after the storm, recovery remains far from complete. Helene caused nearly $60 billion in damage and recovery needs , and about $10 billion in federal assistance has been provided so far. item.title: Trump Vows to Send Election “Monitors” to Maine After Far-Right Conspiracies Spread
item.description:
With voters set to cast ballots in two critical races that could help determine control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, fears of potential voter suppression are running high in Maine. Officials in the state have prepared for months against the possibility of election interference from federal officials, and the state remains on high alert in the run-up to the general election on November 3. Training materials were updated this year to include references to federal statutes barring armed federal agents from polling sites. Training materials for law enforcement officials in the state, obtained by The Intercept through a public records request, were updated this year for the elections to include explicit references to federal statutes barring armed federal agents from polling sites.
